27.1.intro: Your business structure changes how you pay tax and what you're personally on the hook for. A good accountant pays for themselves.

steps.say: Learn the two roles. A bookkeeper keeps records up to date weekly or monthly. An accountant or tax agent prepares returns, gives tax advice and helps you plan.
steps.check: You know which helper does what.

steps.say:
Ask every candidate the same three questions.

- How many online stores do you look after?
- How do you handle Shopify payouts, stock and product cost?
- What does the monthly fee include?
steps.check: You can compare them on the same answers.
steps.lost: Ask: how many online stores do you look after?

steps.say: Choose a fixed monthly fee, with a written list of what's included and what costs extra (like tax returns or catch-up work).
steps.check: No surprise bills.
steps.lost: Ask for the fee in writing.

steps.say: Ask for read-only access to your books from day one, and a short monthly summary.
steps.check: You can see your books any time.

steps.say: Review your structure with your accountant once profit is steady.
steps.check: Your structure still suits the business.
steps.careful: Outside the US: check BAS agents and tax agents on the Tax Practitioners Board register. Common structures are sole trader, company and trust. US: look for a CPA or enrolled agent. Non-residents owning a US company need a cross-border specialist.
steps.lost: Book one chat when profit is steady.

27.2.intro: Copying every order into your accounts makes thousands of lines that never match your bank. Record each payout as one summary instead.

steps.say: Use one accounting system, like Xero or QuickBooks.
steps.check: All records live in one place.

steps.say: Install a connector app that records each payout as one entry, split into sales, shipping charged, discounts, refunds, GST or sales tax, and fees.
steps.check: Each payout is one tidy entry. Compare connectors on price and payment method support.

steps.say: Make a clearing account (a holding account) for each payment provider: Shopify Payments, PayPal, and each buy now pay later provider.
steps.check: Sales go in, payouts and fees come out, and the balance falls back towards zero.

steps.say: Record payment and buy now pay later fees as expenses, not as lower sales.
steps.check: Your sales figure is the full amount.

steps.say: Reconcile (match to the bank) every bank line weekly.
steps.check: Ten minutes a week, nothing left at year end.

steps.say: Each month, compare your books' profit with Helix. Find the reason for any big gap.
steps.check: The two agree, or you know why (usually missing costs or stock changes).
steps.careful: Outside the US: check GST codes, especially on overseas costs with no GST. US: keep sales tax in its own liability account, never in sales.

27.3.intro: Stock you hold is something you own (an asset), not an expense, until it sells. Getting this right is the biggest gap between book profit and real profit.

steps.say: Record stock purchases at landed cost: product price plus freight, duty and broker fees, without claimable GST.
steps.check: Stock values are complete and ex GST.
steps.lost: Price + freight + duty + fees, no GST.

steps.say: Each month or quarter, work out COGS (cost of goods sold): opening stock + purchases − closing stock. Example: $10,000 + $4,000 − $9,000 = $5,000.
steps.check: You have COGS for the period.

steps.say: Count all stock at least once a year (a stocktake). Adjust your books to match.
steps.check: Books match the shelf.

steps.say: Write off damaged, lost or unsellable stock, with a note of why. Ask your accountant how to value slow stock.
steps.check: Dead stock no longer counts as an asset.
steps.lost: List the stock that will never sell.

steps.say: Use the same method every year.
steps.check: Years compare fairly.
steps.careful: Outside the US: count on or near 30 June. Small businesses whose stock value changes by $5,000 or less may skip the formal adjustment. US: count on or near 31 December or your year end.
steps.lost: Write down the method you use.

27.4.intro: A short monthly routine (the monthly close) keeps tax time easy and gives you numbers you can trust. Aim to finish within two weeks of month end.

steps.say: Reconcile all bank accounts, cards and payment clearing accounts.
steps.check: Every balance matches.

steps.say: Attach a receipt or invoice to every expense. Use a receipt app, or forward emails to your accounting software.
steps.check: No expense is missing a receipt.

steps.say: Fix all uncategorised lines.
steps.check: Every line has a category.

steps.say: Compare profit and loss with last month and with Helix.
steps.check: Changes make sense.

steps.say: Move tax money (GST or sales tax, plus an income tax estimate) into a separate savings account.
steps.check: Tax is set aside.
steps.lost: Move the GST amount to savings.

steps.say: Save key reports into a folder for the year.
steps.check: The year's records are in one place.
steps.careful: Outside the US: keep most records for 5 years. US: keep them at least 3 years, and employment tax records 4 years.
steps.lost: Save your profit and loss report.

27.5.intro: Some financial years end on 30 June. Helix puts these steps on your calendar from May, so nothing is rushed.

steps.say: In early May, book a planning chat with your accountant about expected profit and tax.
steps.check: The meeting is booked.
steps.lost: Email your accountant to book a chat.

steps.say:
Before 30 June, finish the year-end jobs.

1. Count your stock (stocktake).
2. Write off stock that will never sell.
3. Make sure team super is paid on time.
steps.check: Stock and super are done.
steps.careful: From 1 July 2026, employers pay super with each payday, and it must reach the fund within 7 business days.

steps.say: Before 30 June, gather receipts for big purchases. Check which costs fall in this year.
steps.check: Deductions are documented.

steps.say: In July, reconcile every account to 30 June. Send your accountant the year's reports.
steps.check: Your accountant has everything.

steps.say: Lodge the June quarter BAS by 28 July. Lodging online may add two weeks, and agents may have later dates.
steps.check: BAS is lodged.

steps.say: Lodge your income tax return by 31 October yourself. Or be on a registered tax agent's client list before then, to lodge later.
steps.check: Your return date is known and met.
steps.lost: Using an agent? Join their list before 31 October.

27.6.intro: Most US stores run on the calendar year. Helix puts these dates on your calendar for US stores.

steps.say: In December, count stock. Check your sales tax registrations against each state's threshold.
steps.check: Stock is counted and registrations are up to date.

steps.say: Collect a Form W-9 from every contractor before you pay them.
steps.check: You have a W-9 for each contractor.
steps.lost: Ask each contractor for a W-9.

steps.say: By 31 January, send Form 1099-NEC to contractors paid $2,000 or more in 2026, and file it with the IRS. (The 2025 limit was $600.)
steps.check: All 1099s are sent and filed. Payment providers send a 1099-K once you pass $20,000 across more than 200 payments.
steps.lost: Paid someone $2,000 or more? Send a 1099-NEC.

steps.say: By 15 March, file partnership and S corporation returns (next business day if it's a weekend).
steps.check: Those returns are filed.

steps.say: By 15 April, file individual and C corporation returns and pay the first estimated tax. Later estimates fall on 15 June, 15 September and 15 January.
steps.check: Returns are filed and estimates are in your calendar.
steps.careful: Foreign-owned US companies have extra forms, such as Form 5472, so use a cross-border specialist.
